\chapter{Me Lo --- Both at Once}
\label{ch:double-object-order}
\hlchaptermodality{98}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can put two object pronouns in front of one verb, in the right order.}

Complete ES-C47-me-lo: produce te lo digo and me la haces, and say which pronoun leads.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[me lo]{me lo — both at once}

\label{lesson:ES-C47-me-lo}



\begin{quote}
You have a pronoun for the \textbf{thing} and a pronoun for the \textbf{person}. A sentence often needs both. What happens then?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: they stand together, in one order}]
They queue up in the same slot, both still in front of the verb:

\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{Me lo} dices.} — You tell \textbf{it} \textbf{to me}. \emph{\textbf{Te lo} digo.} — I tell \textbf{it} \textbf{to you}.
\end{quote}

Two small words, one after the other, and then the verb. Nothing has moved.

\textbf{The order never varies.} The person comes first, then the thing:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{indirect, then direct.} \emph{Me lo}, never \emph{lo me}.
\end{quote}

That is the entire rule, and it is worth noticing what it saves you. English lets you choose — \emph{give it to me} or \emph{give me it} — and the choice carries a faint difference in emphasis you have to feel your way into. Spanish took the choice away. There is one order, it is always right, and you never have to decide.

A fixed order is a smaller thing to learn than a free one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Me lo dices\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Te lo digo\textquotedblright{} — hear the pair stay glued
  \item \textquotedblleft{}me la haces\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}I tell it to you\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Te lo digo}}.) Which pronoun leads? (The \textbf{person} — indirect first.) Next: the one combination Spanish refuses to say, and what it says instead.
\end{tcolorbox}
